title: Introduction and Architecture
content:
Overview In an e-commerce application, placing an order triggers several downstream tasks: recording the order, sending a confirmation email, and notifying administrators. If all of these are handled within the same request (synchronously), the system slows down easily as order volume grows, and a failure in a secondary service can cause lost orders or duplicate emails.
This workshop builds an order-processing flow that is event-driven, fault-tolerant, and observable on AWS, then runs measurements to compare it against a synchronous approach.
The problem to solve A synchronous API may wait for database writes and email submission before responding. A slow or failing task can delay the response or return an error. If the visitor retries, the application must distinguish a new order from another attempt to submit the same order.
An asynchronous design separates acceptance from completion. The API places a request in a queue, while downstream components continue processing it. This requires clear order states, duplicate controls and observable failures.
Design principles Track by order ID: correlate requests, database records and executions using the same identifier. Expect redelivery: SQS Standard does not guarantee that a message is delivered only once. Persist processing state: acceptance is not completion. Use multiple evidence sources: combine logs, DynamoDB, execution history and received email. The four subsections explain the intended deliverables, architecture, evaluation approach and time/cost plan. Understand the design before deploying resources. This introductory section does not require additional Console screenshots or new resources.

title: Create the template.yaml file
content:
← Section contents
Write the complete template.yaml In PowerShell, start in the order-system application directory and run the blocks in order. File writers use UTF-8 without a BOM. Save local customizations before replacing a file of the same name.
$content = @' AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09' Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31 Description: Order workshop - SQS and DLQ Resources: OrdersDLQ: Type: AWS::SQS::Queue Properties: MessageRetentionPeriod: 1209600 # keep failed messages for 14 days OrdersQueue: Type: AWS::SQS::Queue Properties: VisibilityTimeout: 60 RedrivePolicy: deadLetterTargetArn: !GetAtt OrdersDLQ.Arn maxReceiveCount: 3 Outputs: QueueUrl: Value: !Ref OrdersQueue DlqUrl: Value: !Ref OrdersDLQ '@ $path = Join-Path $PWD.Path 'template.yaml' [IO.File]::WriteAllText($path, ($content + [Environment]::NewLine), [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) Read the dead-letter queue before the source queue OrdersDLQ sets retention to 1,209,600 seconds, or 14 days. For a Standard queue, retention still depends on the original enqueue time after transfer to the DLQ. A longer retention gives an operator time to investigate. The transfer itself does not reset the full retention interval.
In OrdersQueue, deadLetterTargetArn refers to the ARN of the OrdersDLQ resource in this template. The physical queue names can differ between accounts. Linking by logical ID preserves the relationship on each deployment. The outputs expose URLs because SQS uses a queue URL for send, receive and attribute operations.
Trace a delivery attempt Suppose a consumer receives a message at 10:00:00. With a 60-second visibility timeout, other consumers ordinarily cannot see that message during the interval. Deleting it after processing completes the delivery. Leaving it undeleted makes redelivery possible when the interval expires. An actual receive increases the receive count. Waiting beside an idle queue does not make a message move toward the DLQ.
Read the saved file before building Get-Item -LiteralPath .\template.yaml -ErrorAction Stop | Select-Object FullName, Length Select-String -LiteralPath .\template.yaml -Pattern '^ (OrdersQueue|OrdersDLQ|QueueUrl|DlqUrl):' Locate the two resource IDs and two output names at their intended indentation levels. If the file is missing, return to the application directory from 5.2.6. This part of the exercise is local and can be checked before provisioning SQS.

title: IAM permissions
content:
← Section contents
Run the block in Windows PowerShell to place only the policy JSON on the clipboard. Open IAM → Policies → Create policy → JSON, paste and name it OrderWorkshopDeployPolicy.
$policyJson = @' { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "WorkshopServices", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "cloudformation:*", "lambda:*", "sqs:*", "dynamodb:*", "states:*", "sns:*", "ses:*", "cloudwatch:*", "logs:*", "events:*", "s3:*" ], "Resource": "*" }, { "Sid": "WorkshopIam", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "iam:CreateRole", "iam:DeleteRole", "iam:GetRole", "iam:PassRole", "iam:TagRole", "iam:UntagRole", "iam:AttachRolePolicy", "iam:DetachRolePolicy", "iam:PutRolePolicy", "iam:DeleteRolePolicy", "iam:GetRolePolicy", "iam:ListRolePolicies", "iam:ListAttachedRolePolicies" ], "Resource": "*" } ] } '@ $null = $policyJson | ConvertFrom-Json -ErrorAction Stop Set-Clipboard -Value $policyJson This policy is broad for the convenience of the test environment. For a real environment, restrict the Resource to each specific resource.
Deployment permissions versus runtime permissions The CLI identity needs permission to create or update resources in the template. At runtime, Lambda and Step Functions use their own execution roles. Access to the Console does not establish that the application roles have every required permission.
Component Example responsibilities requiring permission Deployment identity CloudFormation and template services; create/pass roles where required Worker Lambda Process SQS messages, access DynamoDB and start the workflow Step Functions Call SES, update DynamoDB and publish to SNS as defined by its states The example policy is broad for a lab environment. For other uses, restrict actions and resources to the actual ARNs. API and storefront extensions require permissions matching their own templates.
Investigating AccessDenied Open the active user or role in IAM and inspect Permissions. For a failure, record the identity, action and resource in the AWS error. Do not assume every AccessDenied can be solved by attaching a broad policy.
An identity without permission to attach policies to itself needs an authorized administrator to grant appropriate access. A successful STS response establishes identity, not complete deployment permissions.
Reuse an existing Permissions screenshot where appropriate. There is no need to create another user or policy just to obtain an illustration.
Attach the policy to the identity used for deployment In IAM, open the user used by the order-workshop profile and inspect Permissions. If an administrator has provided a group or role with the required access, record that identity for use throughout the lab. For a dedicated lab user, create the policy from the JSON at the top, attach it to that user and check that OrderWorkshopDeployPolicy appears in the permissions list. A billing administrator may handle budget setup separately.
Suppose CloudFormation creates the table and then fails while creating the function. Read the first event that identifies a denied action. A denial of iam:PassRole concerns the identity handing a role to a service. A denial of dynamodb:PutItem in a worker invocation points to the Lambda execution role and the table ARN. The point in the run tells you which identity to inspect.
Record a useful access request Capture the time, Region, stack name, denied action and resource from the error. This gives an administrator enough context to check the policy, permissions boundary and relevant organization controls. Once access is updated, retry the same operation with the same profile. Leave access keys and customer email content out of the incident record.

title: Monitoring objective and architecture
content:
← Section contents
Observe SQS, Lambda and Step Functions with CloudWatch metrics, three alarms, a dashboard and SNS email in ap-southeast-1. The supplementary order-monitoring-evidence stack monitors order-orchestration-evidence application resources.
Observe an order and observe the system Use a DynamoDB key and execution history to locate an individual order. CloudWatch answers a broader question about which component showed symptoms during a time window. A Lambda invocation failure can increment Errors without including an order ID in the datapoint. Keep the timestamp, function name and Region so you can return to the log.
The dashboard groups four signals. Visible messages describe the backlog available to consumers. Oldest-message age highlights prolonged waiting. Execution metrics show workflow starts and outcomes. Lambda invocation and error metrics show worker activity. Backlog rising along with age suggests that arrivals outpaced processing during the selected interval.
Attach monitoring to your deployment The runnable example uses the order-system application and a separate order-monitoring stack. Monitoring receives queue and function names, the state machine ARN and the SNS topic ARN from the application. Names ending in evidence in the illustrations belong to the recorded environment. Resolve your own resources so the dashboard follows the deployment that receives your test traffic.
An alarm can notify on a state transition, while the workflow can publish for an individual failed order. A CloudWatch notification identifies an alarm and threshold. A business notification carries an order ID. Identify the source before using email timestamps for measurement.
Choose a first chart for a delay complaint Suppose customers report a delay without an error alarm. Check oldest-message age and source depth. If both increase while executions succeed, completions may be lagging behind intake. A small source backlog with executions waiting for retries places the delay downstream. The configured alarms target particular errors, so a slow run can still require dashboard inspection.

title: Replace the entire template.yaml
content:
← Section contents
Trace one order through the state definition Begin at StartAt and follow each Next. Input includes at least orderId and customerEmail. In SendCustomerEmail, States.Array creates the recipient list from one address. ResultPath: null retains the input after the SES response, leaving the order ID available to MarkDone. Replacing the input with the SES response could remove the key the next state needs.
On the error path, Catch places the error under $.error while retaining the order ID. MarkFailed updates the item, NotifyAdminFailure publishes the ID and OrderFailed terminates the execution. Inspect both the first failing state and the last state reached. A denial in the failed-status update itself can end the flow before the SNS publish.
Work out the wait before interpreting the result An interval of 2 seconds, backoff of 2 and three retry attempts allow the original call plus three further calls. The waits are 2, 4 and 8 seconds, a total of 14 seconds before service and transition time. If the second call succeeds, the later waits never occur. Record configured retry capacity separately from the attempts observed in history.
The template also introduces two email parameters. SenderEmail sends order confirmations. AdminEmail subscribes to the administrative topic. Checking both values before deployment avoids searching the wrong inbox later.

title: Update template.yaml
content:
← Section contents
Read the three bindings in the template OrdersTable uses a string orderId as its partition key. Two writes for the same purchase target the same item. The worker will supply the conditional write in the next step. The key alone identifies the destination of an operation. With PAY_PER_REQUEST the small lab can use the table without sizing read and write capacity in advance.
In ProcessOrderFn, TABLE_NAME receives the physical table name from CloudFormation. The function policy references the same table. An inconsistent edit could leave the worker authorized for one table while its code addresses another. Handler: index.handler resolves to the exported handler in src/index.mjs.
Picture a one-message batch The SQS event source mapping calls Lambda with a batch. Here BatchSize is one, so a parse error fails processing for one message. The 10-second function timeout and 60-second queue visibility timeout meet the six-times guideline with a zero batching window. Revisit both values if adapting the worker timeout for another exercise.

The table, sender and downstream workflow reuse earlier resources. Keep the same account and Region, and assign distinct ID prefixes to each group so their results stay separable.
The following template is the complete 5.5.1 example with the API changes applied. It preserves the queue, table, worker and state machine logical IDs. Compare local customizations before replacing an edited template. The alarms from 5.6 live in a separate monitoring stack. This application update adds the HTTP functions and ApiUrl output.
Interpret the new item fields createdAt marks the application’s intake time. On the async path doneAt comes from entry into MarkDone. The application increments emailCount with its successful completion update. This is an application-side count. A delivery event or a real mailbox observation answers the separate question of mail arrival.
Exponential backoff with full jitter gives throttled executions different opportunities to retry. With six retries the delay ceilings are 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 seconds. Their total scheduled-wait ceiling is 126 seconds before service call duration. Use the actual execution history for an individual failure.

title: What you will do
content:
← Section contents
Decouple order intake from order processing using Amazon SQS and a dead-letter queue (DLQ) Prevent duplicate processing with Amazon DynamoDB (idempotency) Orchestrate the email and notification workflow with AWS Step Functions, Amazon SES, and Amazon SNS Monitor the system and receive alerts with Amazon CloudWatch Simulate failures and load to evaluate the effectiveness of the architecture Expected deliverables Explain the problem each service addresses, deploy the configuration and verify results using real observations. Resources appearing in the AWS Console are only a starting point; check how they work together.
Activity Expected outcome Verification Accept an order A valid request is accepted and can be tracked API response or storefront Process an order The workflow reaches an appropriate terminal state Execution and DynamoDB record Control duplicates Repeated requests are recognized Logs for the same order and task history Handle failures A failure is recorded with a defined handling path Catch branch, FAILED state or DLQ, depending on the failure Monitor operations The operator identifies the affected resource and time Dashboard, alarm history and notifications Example scenario A visitor orders two cups. The website receives an order ID after acceptance, while email processing continues in the background. If the result of the first submission is uncertain, a retry should preserve the request identity to reduce accidental creation of another order.
Evaluation boundaries Limit conclusions to the tested inputs and observations. A successful duplicate test does not establish exactly-once effects under every possible failure. Record the input, submission count, observation time and actual result.
The objectives table is sufficient here; new screenshots are optional. Capture execution evidence when completing the relevant deployment and experiment sections.
Follow a purchase from checkout to its final state Suppose a customer orders two cups and the browser submits MOC-101. The asynchronous API returns HTTP 202 once SQS accepts the message. The storefront can now show “Order MOC-101 received.” A Lambda invocation may still be waiting to start. The application can report DONE once the workflow submits the email and writes that status to the table.
Now let the connection drop just after checkout. A second click can produce a second SQS MessageId for the same purchase. Reusing the original orderId allows the worker to recognize the retry. A customer who actually wants another two cups needs a new order ID. This distinction affects what you count when you assess duplicate processing later.
Match each question to an observation Reader Question Where to look Customer Has the system accepted my order? The API response and its order ID Support How far has the order progressed? The item under that key and the named workflow execution Operator Where can I investigate a failure? The failing state, or the DLQ body if parsing failed at the worker At the end of the lab, write a three-line account for one order. Record acceptance, the next component to handle it, and the observed outcome. If only the first two events are available, leave the outcome pending.

title: Proposal
content:
Design and Implementation of a Fault-Tolerant, Monitored Event-Driven Order Processing Architecture on AWS, with Experimental Evaluation 1. Background and Problem When a customer places an order in an online store, the system has to do several things: record the order, send a confirmation email, update its status, and alert the operator if something goes wrong. The simplest approach is to cram all of this into a single request (synchronous processing). It is easy to write, but it shows four weaknesses once the system runs for real:
Weakness Symptom Slow responses The customer waits for the entire processing chain, especially when a secondary service (such as email) is slow or rate-limited Lost or stuck orders A failing secondary step fails the whole request, and the order may stop in a half-finished state Duplicate processing The customer clicks submit several times, or the system retries on its own, so one order is processed and emailed multiple times Undetected failures Without monitoring, the operator only finds out when customers complain This project proposes an event-driven architecture on AWS to address these weaknesses, then uses experiments to measure where it is better than the synchronous approach and what trade-offs it brings.
2. Objectives and Scope Objectives
Design and deploy an asynchronous order-processing flow that is fault tolerant, free of duplicate processing, and able to raise alerts. Build a synchronous approach as a baseline, running under the same conditions. Measure and compare the two approaches using quantitative metrics. Write workshop documentation so that others can reproduce it step by step. Scope: the system runs in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1 region, is deployed with AWS SAM, and is tested at loads of 20 and 50 orders. The project does not build a customer-facing web interface, does not handle payments, and does not aim to measure production-scale performance.
3. Proposed Architecture 3.1. Processing flow The customer sends an order to API Gateway (HTTP API); a Lambda function validates the API key and the order format, puts the order into an SQS queue, and immediately returns 202 Accepted. Another Lambda function reads the message from SQS, records the order in DynamoDB (RECEIVED) using a condition that only writes if the order ID does not yet exist, then starts a Step Functions execution named after the order ID. The state machine sends a confirmation email to the customer through Amazon SES, with exponential-backoff retries. On success: update the status to DONE. On failure after retries are exhausted: update the status to FAILED, send an alert through Amazon SNS, and end in a failed state. CloudWatch monitors the entire flow and raises alerts when something abnormal happens. 3.2. Role of each component Component Service Role Entry point API Gateway, Lambda Receive orders, validate them, respond quickly Queue Amazon SQS Decouple order intake from processing, buffer when order volume rises Dead-letter queue SQS DLQ Hold messages that cannot be processed after the maximum receive count Order ledger Amazon DynamoDB Record the status of each order, prevent duplicate processing Orchestration AWS Step Functions Manage each step, with explicit retries and error catching Notification Amazon SES, Amazon SNS Send email to customers and alerts to administrators Monitoring Amazon CloudWatch Alarms and dashboard Deployment AWS SAM (CloudFormation) Describe the whole infrastructure in a single template 4. Fault-Tolerant Design Each type of failure has its own handling mechanism, rather than relying on one generic mechanism:
Failure Handling mechanism Result Malformed message, Lambda error SQS redelivers the message; after 3 receives it moves to the DLQ No message is lost, and it can be inspected and reprocessed The same order submitted several times Conditional write to DynamoDB; execution name equals the order ID An order runs only once, with no second email Temporary email failure (for example SES rate limiting) Step Functions Retry: 6 attempts, backoff rate 2, with jitter Recovers automatically without intervention Permanent email failure Catch routes to MarkFailed and then NotifyAdminFailure The order is marked FAILED and the administrator is notified immediately 5. Monitoring and Alerting The system has three CloudWatch Alarms: messages in the DLQ, a failed Step Functions execution, and Lambda errors. All three send alerts through the same SNS topic. In addition, a dashboard shows queue length, age of the oldest message, Lambda invocations and errors, and Step Functions executions on a single screen, so the operator can see the state of the system at a glance.
6. Experiment Plan Both approaches are deployed in the same stack and use the same API key so that the comparison is fair:
Synchronous (baseline) Asynchronous (proposed) Endpoint POST /sync POST /async How it processes Writes to DynamoDB and then sends via SES within the request Puts the order into SQS, processed in the background by Lambda and Step Functions Duplicate protection, retries, DLQ, alerts No Yes Three experiments
Latency and load: send 20 and 50 orders with several concurrent requests, and measure API response time (average, p95), the number of completed, failed, stuck, or lost orders, and processing completion time. Duplicates: send the same order ID 5 times to each endpoint and count the extra emails. Failures and alerts: use an unverified email so SES rejects it, measure the time from the failure to the alert (directly through SNS and through the CloudWatch Alarm), and check that malformed messages move to the DLQ. Evaluation metrics: average and p95 API response; rate of lost or stuck orders when failures occur; number of duplicate emails; time until an alert is raised on failure; processing completion time; and the actual cost of the whole experiment.
7. Constraints and Risks Constraint or risk Mitigation The SES sandbox limits sending to 1 email/second and only to verified addresses Use the success@simulator.amazonses.com mailbox simulator, cap the load at 20 and 50 orders, and record this as a bottleneck shared by both approaches Two API endpoints exposed to the Internet Protect them with an x-api-key key, keep the key and samconfig.toml out of the repository, and delete the whole stack when finished Measurements fluctuate because of Lambda cold starts and time of day Warm up first, repeat each load level at least 3 times, and take the average Unexpected costs Set up AWS Budgets from the start, clean up resources at the end, and check Cost Explorer after 1 to 2 days 8. Expected Results An order-processing system running on AWS, repeatably deployable with a single sam deploy command. No order is lost when a step fails; failed orders are retained and trigger an alert. An order is processed and emailed only once, even if it is submitted multiple times. A table of real measurements comparing the two approaches, with an honest discussion of strengths and limitations, including the metrics where the asynchronous architecture has no advantage (for example, completion time is usually longer because processing runs in the background). A step-by-step workshop guide covering preparation, SQS and DLQ, duplicate protection, Step Functions, monitoring, experiments, and cleanup. Future work: add a mechanism to reprocess FAILED orders (currently, resubmitting the same ID is treated as a duplicate), and request that SES be moved out of the sandbox to test at larger loads.
9. Duration and Cost The workshop takes about 2 to 3 hours. At test scale, most services fall within the free tier or cost very little; the actual cost will be recorded from Cost Explorer after the run. Set up a cost alert (AWS Budgets) from the start and perform the resource cleanup step at the end to avoid unexpected charges.

title: Architecture
content:
← Section contents
Reading the architecture Follow one order through the diagram. The intake layer places it in SQS. A worker Lambda handles the message and starts Step Functions. DynamoDB supports duplicate control and order status. Step Functions calls SES, then records completion or follows its failure path.
Stage Path Intake API → SQS Processing Lambda → Step Functions → SES Failed delivery SQS → DLQ once the receive threshold is crossed Data and observation DynamoDB stores state, CloudWatch aggregates signals, SNS delivers notifications Responsibilities API: validate and accept input; acceptance is not completed processing. SQS: buffer messages and support redelivery. Lambda: run the application’s message-processing logic. Step Functions: manage task order, retries and error handling. DynamoDB: persist state for tracking and duplicate checks. Connection to the Moc storefront The deployed execute-api website serves its interface through API Gateway, an asset-serving Lambda and a private S3 bucket. Order requests use a separate API Lambda before entering the existing queue. Distinguish the asset-serving function, API function and order-processing worker.
An email failure inside Step Functions does not automatically place the original SQS message in the DLQ. SQS redrive and workflow Catch handling apply at different stages.
Reuse the existing architecture diagram. If it illustrates only the source workflow, state that scope instead of presenting it as the complete storefront hosting architecture. No additional deployment is required for a diagram screenshot.
Locate the two boundaries on the diagram First follow the arrow from SQS to Lambda. A message is temporarily hidden while the worker handles it. When the invocation returns successfully, the SQS integration can delete the message from the source queue. In section 5.5 the worker finishes its part after starting Step Functions. The source queue can therefore be empty while a customer’s email task is still running.
Next follow Step Functions to SES. If SES rejects a request, execution history records the task failure and the configured retries. After exhaustion the workflow writes FAILED and publishes to SNS. The named execution is a good starting point for this incident. A malformed JSON body can fail earlier, before the worker knows an order ID or starts an execution. The Lambda log and the DLQ identify that failure.
Predict the last observable step For one submitted order, establish whether the API enqueued a message, the worker started a named execution, and that execution reached a terminal state. Checking those boundaries in sequence narrows the search even when a dashboard aggregates many orders. Queue URLs and the state machine ARN belong to a particular deployment. Re-read them from the stack when moving to another environment.

Alarm Namespace / metric Dimension Statistic order-monitoring-evidence-sfn-failed AWS/States / ExecutionsFailed StateMachineArn Sum order-monitoring-evidence-lambda-errors AWS/Lambda / Errors FunctionName Sum order-monitoring-evidence-dlq AWS/SQS / ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible DLQ QueueName Maximum All three use threshold > 0, period 60 seconds, EvaluationPeriods 1, DatapointsToAlarm 1 and TreatMissingData notBreaching. AlarmActions and OKActions reference the application’s SNS topic.
Sum counts failures within a period; Maximum detects visible DLQ messages. SQS metrics are approximate. A 60-second period does not guarantee email delivery within 60 seconds. CloudWatch normally notifies on state transitions, rather than for every failure while ALARM persists.
Match dimensions to the signal A metric name identifies a quantity. AWS/SQS publishes it for many queues, so the DLQ alarm needs the destination QueueName. Selecting the source queue would count ordinary pending orders. The Lambda signal uses the physical function name. Step Functions uses the complete state machine ARN. A valid alarm pointed at the wrong dimension set may receive no relevant datapoints.
Sum adds execution or invocation errors within a minute. Maximum takes the highest observed visible-message count in that period. One DLQ message present across two periods can hold the alarm in ALARM for both and generate only the initial transition notification. Two datapoints of one may describe the same message.
Read the template for your own account The PowerShell block writes a local CloudFormation template. Section 5.6.3 supplies live resource identifiers. Interpret a hypothetical evaluation period Suppose the maximum DLQ visible count is zero, one and one across three periods. With a threshold of zero and the greater-than operator, the second period breaches. If the alarm remains in alarm, the third period does not cause a second transition into alarm. Another faulty message can require handling even if the operator receives only one email. This makes the initial alarm state part of the experiment record.

Write the application handler In PowerShell, start in the order-system application directory and run the blocks in order. File writers use UTF-8 without a BOM. Save local customizations before replacing a file of the same name.

The execution name = orderId, so it cannot run twice. try { await sfn.send(new StartExecutionCommand({ stateMachineArn: process.env.STATE_MACHINE_ARN, name: order.orderId, input: JSON.stringify(order), })); console.log("Workflow started:", order.orderId); } catch (e) { if (e.name === "ExecutionAlreadyExists") { console.log("Workflow already exists, skipping:", order.orderId); continue; } throw e; } } }; '@ $path = Join-Path $PWD.Path 'src/index.mjs' [IO.File]::WriteAllText($path, ($content + [Environment]::NewLine), [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) Because orderId is used as the execution name, it should only contain letters, digits, -, and _ (up to 80 characters).
Package the worker dependencies Push-Location -LiteralPath .\src -ErrorAction Stop try { if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath .\package.json)) { npm.cmd init -y if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'npm init failed.' } } npm.cmd install @aws-sdk/client-dynamodb @aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb @aws-sdk/client-sfn if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Dependency installation failed.' } } finally { Pop-Location } Revisit a recorded order that is still RECEIVED The worker performs two separate operations: recording an order and asking Step Functions to start an execution. If the process stops between them, the item can still be RECEIVED on redelivery. After a conditional conflict, the handler reads that item. It attempts startup for RECEIVED and can acknowledge a terminal DONE or FAILED item. The example uses a strongly consistent key read after conflict to observe the completed write.
The execution name comes from orderId. For a running Standard workflow, StartExecution with the same name and input can return the existing execution. Changing the input under the same name can produce ExecutionAlreadyExists. Preserve the business payload when replaying a purchase. Amending a confirmed purchase requires a separately defined operation.
Trace three arrivals through the handler Item at arrival Handler path Observation No item Conditional Put succeeds, then StartExecution An execution named after the ID Existing RECEIVED Read state and attempt startup under the same name History of the named execution Existing terminal state Acknowledge the redelivery Matching log and unchanged terminal state The name constrains startup under the naming and retention rules of Standard workflows. The downstream states record completion and any application counter. Counting “started” log lines alone cannot tell how many emails arrived.

content:
← Section contents
In PowerShell, start in the order-system application directory and run the blocks in order. File writers use UTF-8 without a BOM. Save local customizations before replacing a file of the same name.
Synchronous HTTP function $content = @' import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb"; import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, UpdateCommand } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb"; import { SESv2Client, SendEmailCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-sesv2"; const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({})); const ses = new SESv2Client({}); const ID = /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$/; export const handler = async (event) => { if (event.headers?.["x-api-key"] !== process.env.API_KEY) return { statusCode: 403, body: "forbidden" }; let order; try { order = JSON.parse(event.body); } catch { return { statusCode: 400, body: "invalid json" }; } if (typeof order?.orderId !== "string" || !ID.test(order.orderId) || !order.customerEmail) return { statusCode: 400, body: "invalid order" }; const key = { orderId: order.orderId }; try { await db.send(new UpdateCommand({ TableName: process.env.TABLE_NAME, Key: key, UpdateExpression: "SET #s = :r, createdAt = if_not_exists(createdAt, :c)", ExpressionAttributeNames: { "#s": "status" }, ExpressionAttributeValues: { ":r": "RECEIVED", ":c": Date.now() }, })); await ses.send(new SendEmailCommand({ FromEmailAddress: process.env.SENDER_EMAIL, Destination: { ToAddresses: [order.customerEmail] }, Content: { Simple: { Subject: { Data: `Order confirmation ${order.orderId}` }, Body: { Text: { Data: `Thank you. Your order ${order.orderId} has been received.` } }, } }, })); await db.send(new UpdateCommand({ TableName: process.env.TABLE_NAME, Key: key, UpdateExpression: "SET #s = :d, doneAt = :t ADD emailCount :one", ExpressionAttributeNames: { "#s": "status" }, ExpressionAttributeValues: { ":d": "DONE", ":t": new Date().toISOString(), ":one": 1 }, })); return { statusCode: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ orderId: order.orderId, status: "DONE" }) }; } catch (e) { console.error("Error processing order", order.orderId, e.name); return { statusCode: 500, body: "error" }; } }; '@ $path = Join-Path $PWD.Path 'src/sync-order.mjs' [IO.File]::WriteAllText($path, ($content + [Environment]::NewLine), [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) Asynchronous intake function $content = @' import { SQSClient, SendMessageCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-sqs"; const sqs = new SQSClient({}); const ID = /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$/; export const handler = async (event) => { if (event.headers?.["x-api-key"] !== process.env.API_KEY) return { statusCode: 403, body: "forbidden" }; let order; try { order = JSON.parse(event.body); } catch { return { statusCode: 400, body: "invalid json" }; } if (typeof order?.orderId !== "string" || !ID.test(order.orderId) || !order.customerEmail) return { statusCode: 400, body: "invalid order" }; await sqs.send(new SendMessageCommand({ QueueUrl: process.env.QUEUE_URL, MessageBody: JSON.stringify({ orderId: order.orderId, customerEmail: order.customerEmail, acceptedAt: Date.now(), }), })); return { statusCode: 202, body: JSON.stringify({ orderId: order.orderId, status: "ACCEPTED" }) }; }; '@ $path = Join-Path $PWD.Path 'src/async-order.mjs' [IO.File]::WriteAllText($path, ($content + [Environment]::NewLine), [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) Preserve the acceptance time in the worker This is the complete 5.5.2 src/index.mjs worker with its updated createdAt value.
$content = @' import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb"; import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, PutCommand, GetCommand, } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb"; import { SFNClient, StartExecutionCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-sfn"; const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({})); const sfn = new SFNClient({}); export const handler = async (event) => { for (const record of event.Records) { const order = JSON.parse(record.body); // invalid JSON -> error -> retry -> DLQ // Step 1: write to the ledger; each orderId may only be written once try { await db.send(new PutCommand({ TableName: process.env.TABLE_NAME, Item: { orderId: order.orderId, status: "RECEIVED", createdAt: order.acceptedAt ?? Date.now() }, ConditionExpression: "attribute_not_exists(orderId)", })); } catch (e) { if (e.name !== "ConditionalCheckFailedException") throw e; const { Item } = await db.send(new GetCommand({ TableName: process.env.TABLE_NAME, Key: { orderId: order.orderId }, ConsistentRead: true, })); if (Item?.status !== "RECEIVED") { console.log("Duplicate order, skipping:", order.orderId); continue; } // Still in RECEIVED state: the previous attempt failed to start the workflow -> retry } // Step 2: start the workflow. The execution name = orderId, so it cannot run twice. try { await sfn.send(new StartExecutionCommand({ stateMachineArn: process.env.STATE_MACHINE_ARN, name: order.orderId, input: JSON.stringify(order), })); console.log("Workflow started:", order.orderId); } catch (e) { if (e.name === "ExecutionAlreadyExists") { console.log("Workflow already exists, skipping:", order.orderId); continue; } throw e; } } }; '@ $path = Join-Path $PWD.Path 'src/index.mjs' [IO.File]::WriteAllText($path, ($content + [Environment]::NewLine), [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) Add the HTTP handlers’ SDK clients Push-Location -LiteralPath .\src -ErrorAction Stop try { if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath .\package.json)) { npm.cmd init -y if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'npm init failed.' } } npm.cmd install @aws-sdk/client-sqs @aws-sdk/client-sesv2 if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Dependency installation failed.' } } finally { Pop-Location } Interpret each endpoint’s response contract Both handlers check the header key, parse JSON and validate the order identifier before touching the queue or table. Letters, digits, hyphens and underscores are suitable for the execution name. The sync success path returns 200 after completing its operations within the request. The async path returns 202 after SQS accepts the body. A 2xx response means the corresponding endpoint reached its own success boundary.
If SES rejects after the sync function wrote RECEIVED, the API may return 500 while an item exists. Report item presence and completed processing separately. For the async path, workflow failure can happen after the client has received 202. Query final states for the correct prefix to determine the outcome.
Use a consistent timestamp convention On /async, acceptedAt is recorded before the SQS send and accompanies the body to the worker. The worker uses it for createdAt when present. Earlier direct-to-queue test messages may omit that field, so the worker retains a current-time fallback. The sync handler records its start inside the request. Client-side API latency and the difference between stored application timestamps therefore have different starting boundaries.
Check the syntax of all three files after writing them. Dependency resolution and service permissions still need the subsequent build and small deployment test.
node --check .\src\sync-order.mjs node --check .\src\async-order.mjs node --check .\src\index.mjs

title: Write the Lambda code
content:
← Section contents
Write the application handler In PowerShell, start in the order-system application directory and run the blocks in order. File writers use UTF-8 without a BOM. Save local customizations before replacing a file of the same name.
$content = @' import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb"; import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, PutCommand } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb"; const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({})); export const handler = async (event) => { for (const record of event.Records) { const order = JSON.parse(record.body); // invalid JSON throws an error -> retry -> DLQ try { await db.send(new PutCommand({ TableName: process.env.TABLE_NAME, Item: { orderId: order.orderId, status: "PROCESSING", createdAt: Date.now(), }, // Only write if the orderId does not exist yet ConditionExpression: "attribute_not_exists(orderId)", })); } catch (e) { if (e.name === "ConditionalCheckFailedException") { console.log("Duplicate order, skipping:", order.orderId); continue; } throw e; } console.log("Processed:", order.orderId); } }; '@ $path = Join-Path $PWD.Path 'src/index.mjs' [IO.File]::WriteAllText($path, ($content + [Environment]::NewLine), [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) The key point is the ConditionExpression: DynamoDB only allows the write if the orderId does not already exist, so the second write is rejected and the Lambda skips that order.
In section 5.5 we will add an order status (PROCESSING → DONE) to handle the case where the order was recorded in the ledger but the email-sending step failed.
Package the worker dependencies Push-Location -LiteralPath .\src -ErrorAction Stop try { if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath .\package.json)) { npm.cmd init -y if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'npm init failed.' } } npm.cmd install @aws-sdk/client-dynamodb @aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Dependency installation failed.' } } finally { Pop-Location } Put the condition on the write itself Imagine two invocations receiving A001. A separate read followed by a write would let both check before either item exists. DynamoDB evaluates attribute_not_exists(orderId) as part of Put. One write wins and the other receives ConditionalCheckFailedException. The check applies to the target item, so unrelated order IDs remain independent.
Read the catch branches separately. A condition failure logs the ID and lets the batch complete. The SQS integration can acknowledge processing. Another exception propagates out of the worker so the message can be delivered again. Treating a denied DynamoDB write as a duplicate could acknowledge a new order that had never been recorded.
Establish the boundary of this worker After the first successful Put, the item contains createdAt and PROCESSING. If the process stops immediately afterward, the next delivery finds an existing key. This version has no workflow to resume an email operation, so the result proves that an order marker was written. Section 5.5 introduces RECEIVED and a named execution to handle startup after recording.
Check the JavaScript syntax locally after writing the file. This check does not invoke the handler or consume a message.

title: Connect your computer to your AWS account
content:
← Section contents
Go to IAM → Users → select the user → Security credentials → Create access key (use case: Command Line Interface). Configure the profile: aws configure --profile order-workshop $env:AWS_PROFILE = "order-workshop" aws sts get-caller-identity Enter the Access Key, Secret Key, region ap-southeast-1, and output json. The result of the last command should display your account information.
Do not push the Access Key to GitHub. Delete or deactivate the key after you finish the workshop.
Verify the actual CLI identity and Region The Console and CLI may use different identities. Check which account the CLI actually accesses before deployment. If your organization provides IAM Identity Center access, use its profile instructions instead of creating an extra access key just to follow an example.
For an already configured order-workshop profile:
aws sts get-caller-identity --profile order-workshop --region ap-southeast-1 --query '{Account:Account,Arn:Arn}' --output table --no-cli-pager aws configure get region --profile order-workshop The first command should return the intended Account and Arn. The second reads the Region stored in the profile. Empty output means that value is not stored there; it does not confirm the Console Region. Specifying –region ap-southeast-1 makes the intended Region explicit.
Avoid deploying to the wrong environment Use the same profile throughout. Recheck AWS_PROFILE after opening another terminal, since a variable set in the previous session may not persist. Refresh an expired session for ExpiredToken errors. If STS succeeds but a service returns AccessDenied, inspect that service’s permissions.
Do not include access keys, secret keys or session tokens in source code or screenshots. Existing working access can be checked without generating another key.
An identity screenshot should show the STS result and configured Region, with personal account information redacted as needed. SES identity verification is not a substitute for this CLI identity check.
Resume in a new PowerShell session Profile settings persist on disk. Environment variables set in a PowerShell window apply to that session and its child processes. At the start of a new session for sections 5.3–5.7, run the following block. Replace the profile name on the first line if your class provided a different one.
$env:AWS_PROFILE = 'order-workshop' $env:AWS_REGION = 'ap-southeast-1' $env:AWS_DEFAULT_REGION = $env:AWS_REGION aws sts get-caller-identity --output table --no-cli-pager Compare Account with your lab account. An assumed-role ARN includes a session name at the end. If an IAM Identity Center session has expired, sign in again with the same profile and repeat the check. Choosing Singapore in the browser changes the Console view. The environment settings also direct CLI commands and the later Node.js benchmark to Singapore.
Investigate an apparently missing stack Check the active profile, the Region used for the call and the recorded stack name, in that order. Stack names can recur across Regions. A successful STS call and an empty SQS list can both be correct if the resources were created elsewhere. Start deployment when both the account and Region agree with your session notes.

title: Deploy
content:
← Section contents
sam validate --region ap-southeast-1 if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Template validation failed.' } sam build if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Build failed.' } sam deploy --guided --region ap-southeast-1 --no-fail-on-empty-changeset if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Inspect the CloudFormation deployment events.' } Keep the same answers as last time. When asked for the two parameters, enter:
Parameter Value SenderEmail The email verified in section 5.2 AdminEmail The email that receives alerts (can be the same email as above) Confirm the SNS subscription: AWS sends an email titled AWS Notification - Subscription Confirmation to AdminEmail. Open the email and click Confirm subscription, otherwise you will not receive alerts.
Check the two kinds of email confirmation Before building, select your workshop profile and enter the orchestration template directory. Compare SenderEmail with the identity verified in Singapore. Use an inbox someone can monitor during the lab for AdminEmail. Both values may refer to one inbox, although SES identity verification and SNS subscription confirmation are separate service operations.
When the stack finishes, confirm the SNS registration for the intended topic. Inspect its state with the block below, which resolves the topic ARN from the stack logical ID. A ready email subscription shows its ARN. PendingConfirmation means the publisher can use the topic while the email endpoint still awaits its owner’s confirmation.
$topic = aws cloudformation describe-stack-resource --stack-name order-system --logical-resource-id OrderTopic --region ap-southeast-1 --query 'StackResourceDetail.PhysicalResourceId' --output text --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'OrderTopic was not found.' } aws sns list-subscriptions-by-topic --topic-arn $topic --region ap-southeast-1 --query 'Subscriptions[].{Channel:Protocol,Subscription:SubscriptionArn}' --output table --no-cli-pager Verify the bindings before sending an order Read StateMachineArn and TableName in stack outputs. Locate the physical worker in Resources and check its STATE_MACHINE_ARN and TABLE_NAME settings against those outputs. A missing parameter during deployment calls for a guided deploy from this template with both email values. Once the bindings agree, send one valid order before starting duplicate and failure tests.
Reuse an inbox from preparation The inbox may contain two AWS confirmation messages. SES verifies the address as an identity for the selected Region. SNS identifies a topic and offers a subscription-confirmation action. Check that the topic matches the deployed OrderTopic. If an update creates a different topic ARN, confirmation for an older topic does not migrate the subscription.

content:
← Section contents
Key for the API deployment On first deployment the block generates a session key and copies it to the clipboard. To reuse an existing key, set the session’s API_KEY to the current value first.
if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($env:API_KEY)) { $env:API_KEY = [guid]::NewGuid().ToString('N') } Set-Clipboard -Value $env:API_KEY Keep order-system and the existing email values in guided deployment. Paste the clipboard value at the ApiKey prompt. Both APIs use an application key. Keep the key and samconfig.toml local.
sam validate --region ap-southeast-1 if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Template validation failed.' } sam build if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Build failed.' } Set-Clipboard -Value $env:API_KEY sam deploy --guided --region ap-southeast-1 --no-fail-on-empty-changeset if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Inspect the CloudFormation deployment events.' } Resolve the new deployment outputs $stackData = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Cannot read order-system.' } $outputs = @{} foreach ($item in ($stackData | Out-String | ConvertFrom-Json).Stacks[0].Outputs) { $outputs[$item.OutputKey] = $item.OutputValue } $api = $outputs['ApiUrl'] if (-not $api) { throw 'Missing output: ApiUrl' } $table = $outputs['TableName'] if (-not $table) { throw 'Missing output: TableName' } $sm = $outputs['StateMachineArn'] if (-not $sm) { throw 'Missing output: StateMachineArn' } $env:AWS_REGION = 'ap-southeast-1' $api = $api.TrimEnd('/') Separate deployment settings from benchmark settings ApiKey is the CloudFormation parameter checked against x-api-key by both functions. $env:API_KEY supplies the header value to the benchmark process in this shell. The values must match. NoEcho masks the parameter in certain CloudFormation views. Guided-deployment settings and local shell history still need careful handling. When redeploying without intending to rotate the key, use the current value so this session’s tools remain usable.
ApiUrl is the base URL. Append /async or /sync once per call. Obtain the base URL from the same stack that supplies TableName and StateMachineArn. Physical names in the recorded evidence can differ from your account.
Send one request before a measured run $smokeId = 'smoke-' + [guid]::NewGuid().ToString('N').Substring(0,10) $body = @{ orderId = $smokeId; customerEmail = 'success@simulator.amazonses.com' } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress $response = Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Method Post -Uri "$api/async" -Headers @{'x-api-key' = $env:API_KEY} -ContentType 'application/json' -Body $body -ErrorAction Stop $response | Select-Object StatusCode, Content Read the status and body. The async route should return 202 with the ID just sent. Look up that ID in DynamoDB or Step Functions before measuring a group. For 403 check the session key. For 404 inspect the base URL, route and POST method. For 500 inspect the relevant function log. Keep this smoke request outside the measured population.

title: Evaluation metrics
content:
← Section contents
Response time of the order API (average, p95) Rate of orders lost when failures occur Number of duplicate emails sent Time from when a failure occurs until an administrator receives an alert Separate the timing measurements API response time runs from request submission to response receipt. In an asynchronous flow, that response may only confirm acceptance. Completion time ends when the order reaches its terminal state. Email receipt also includes delivery after SES accepts the message.
Metric Meaning Evidence source Mean API latency Average response time within the run Request-generation tool API P95 A response-time percentile representing the slower requests The same tool and percentile method across runs DONE / FAILED / processing Order states at the observation time DynamoDB and executions Email tasks / received messages Different counts that require separate checks Execution history / recipient inbox Alert delay Time between a defined failure point and a defined alert point Execution, alarm history or email Record comparable experiments Record the run ID, request count, concurrency, pauses, start time and reconciliation time. Compare implementations under equivalent conditions and use the same P95 calculation. Small samples characterize the tested run, not large-scale capacity.
A record not found at one observation does not establish permanent loss. Correlate the API response, queue and logs, then check again after an appropriate wait. An alarm entering ALARM and an email arriving in the inbox are different timestamps.
Suggested recording fields: run ID, requests, successful API responses, DONE, FAILED, unfinished, mean API latency, API P95 and observation time. No load run or additional screenshot is required in this introductory section.
Calculate a percentile for a small run Take 20 HTTP responses and sort their durations from shortest to longest. The nearest-rank P95 is observation number 19, counting from one, because the ceiling of 0.95 × 20 is 19. A very slow twentieth response may pull up the mean while leaving P95 unchanged. Record the number of measured responses beside the percentile. A network exception that produced no HTTP response belongs in the network error count.
Choose the denominator before reporting completion For a worked example, submit 20 distinct IDs and receive 20 acceptances. At the one-minute check the table contains 17 DONE, one FAILED and two RECEIVED. Completion at that instant is 17/20. Both pending orders are traceable. Recheck after the workflow has had time to retry, and keep a second timestamped row. These figures illustrate the calculation only.
For the duplicate test, five submissions of one ID represent five attempts and one purchase. Record requests, distinct IDs, executions and successful email tasks separately. A table containing a single item can otherwise conceal more than one email operation.

title: Queues and DLQ
content:
Objective Create a main queue that receives orders and a dead-letter queue (DLQ) to keep messages that fail processing, instead of losing them.
Three concepts to remember:
Visibility timeout: the time a message stays hidden after a consumer receives it. If the consumer does not delete the message within this time, the message becomes visible again so it can be retried. maxReceiveCount: the number of times a message can be received without being deleted before it is moved to the DLQ. DLQ: a queue that holds failed messages so they can be inspected and reprocessed. Workshop steps Open a page below or use the sidebar. Follow the steps in order.
5.3.1 Create the template.yaml file 5.3.2 Deploy 5.3.3 Verify in the Console 5.3.4 Test a message falling into the DLQ 5.3.5 Verify the result

title: Redeploy
content:
← Section contents
sam validate --region ap-southeast-1 if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Template validation failed.' } sam build if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Build failed.' } sam deploy --region ap-southeast-1 --no-fail-on-empty-changeset if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Inspect the CloudFormation deployment events.' } Verify that the update reads the intended queue After deploying to the existing stack, open CloudFormation → Resources. The two queues from 5.3 should remain in the stack. This update adds the table, worker and event source mapping. The deployment consumes build output, so editing src/index.mjs after a build requires another build before deploying that edit.
The first command below resolves ProcessOrderFn to its physical name. The second reads mappings for that function. Look for Enabled, a source ARN ending in the deployed OrdersQueue name, and a batch size of one.
$worker = aws cloudformation describe-stack-resource --stack-name order-system --logical-resource-id ProcessOrderFn --region ap-southeast-1 --query 'StackResourceDetail.PhysicalResourceId' --output text --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'ProcessOrderFn was not found.' } aws lambda list-event-source-mappings --function-name $worker --region ap-southeast-1 --query 'EventSourceMappings[].{State:State,Source:EventSourceArn,Batch:BatchSize}' --output table --no-cli-pager Allow the trigger to reach its ready state Just after deployment a mapping may still be Creating or Enabling. Wait briefly and read the same mapping again. For an empty list, compare the stack events, profile, Region and function name. If enabled with no invocations, check whether the source has messages. The next test uses a distinct order ID to exercise the whole path.
UPDATE_COMPLETE gives an infrastructure checkpoint. A log line for a new ID and a matching PROCESSING item add two application checkpoints. Keeping all three distinguishes a successful deployment from a worker reading the wrong input.
Match the worker’s table to the test target Read TABLE_NAME in Lambda → Configuration → Environment variables and TableName in CloudFormation Outputs. Matching values establish that the next test will read the table targeted by the worker. If they differ, check whether the function comes from an older stack in the same Region. OrdersTable is the template’s logical ID. The application accesses a physical table name.

title: Verify in the Console
content:
← Section contents
Go to Amazon SQS → Queues. You will see two queues whose names start with order-system-. Open the main queue → Dead-letter queue tab: the dead-letter queue is attached, with Maximum receives = 3. Compare the deployed values with the template Open the source queue identified by QueueUrl and read the destination ARN in its redrive policy. Then open the queue identified by DlqUrl and read its own ARN. Compare the full values. Similar name suffixes can belong to different deployments in the same account.
$raw = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Cannot read the application stack.' } $outputs = ($raw | Out-String | ConvertFrom-Json).Stacks[0].Outputs $q = ($outputs | Where-Object OutputKey -eq 'QueueUrl').OutputValue $dlq = ($outputs | Where-Object OutputKey -eq 'DlqUrl').OutputValue $main = aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url $q --attribute-names RedrivePolicy VisibilityTimeout --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Cannot read the source queue.' } $attrs = ($main | Out-String | ConvertFrom-Json).Attributes $policy = $attrs.RedrivePolicy | ConvertFrom-Json $actualArn = aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url $dlq --attribute-names QueueArn --query 'Attributes.QueueArn' --region ap-southeast-1 --output text --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Cannot read the DLQ.' } [pscustomobject]@{ ConfiguredTarget = $policy.deadLetterTargetArn ActualTarget = $actualArn SameTarget = ($policy.deadLetterTargetArn -eq $actualArn) MaxReceives = $policy.maxReceiveCount VisibilitySeconds = $attrs.VisibilityTimeout } Expect SameTarget to be True, MaxReceives to be 3 and VisibilitySeconds to be 60. The AWS CLI returns the redrive policy as a JSON string inside the outer JSON attribute response. The two JSON parsing steps reflect these two layers.
Resolve a mismatch before polling If both queues exist but the policy is empty, check whether you opened the DLQ as the source. If the destination ARN belongs to another queue, use the stack Resources tab to match each logical ID to its physical name. For a missing queue, read the outputs again in Singapore and verify the profile. Continue to the redelivery experiment after identifying the actual destination. A row with the two ARNs and the receive limit records the configuration for this run.
Hand the queue pair to another operator Give the operator the stack, Region and output names. They can resolve the current URLs with their own profile and read both sets of attributes. Stored URLs can become obsolete when a stack is recreated. Resolving the outputs catches this before the first send. If SameTarget is false, investigate the source-to-DLQ wiring before introducing any failures.
