title: Duration and cost
content:
← Section contents
Planning the work The following ranges are planning estimates, not measured completion times. Actual duration depends on installed tools, available permissions and any environment issues that need troubleshooting.
Activity Suggested time Read the architecture and check tools/identity 30–45 minutes Deploy queues, duplicate controls and orchestration 60–90 minutes Test failures, dashboards and alarms 30–60 minutes Collect evidence and clean up 20–30 minutes Potential cost drivers Charges depend on API requests, Lambda invocations and duration, DynamoDB/SQS requests, Step Functions state transitions, SES messages, logs and CloudWatch resources. The storefront also uses hosting resources such as S3 and Lambda/API Gateway.
Do not assume that every service is free for the lab. Free Tier benefits and credits depend on the account and applicable program. Rounded or delayed Cost Explorer data does not establish a final cost of zero.
Controlling usage Start with a small test, avoid continuous submission loops, configure a budget and record the stacks you create. Clean up when evidence has been saved and the demonstration is no longer needed. Review retained resources and resources created outside the stacks separately.
The USD 5 workshop budget shown in section 5.2.5 is a configured budget amount, not the actual cost of this workshop. There is no need to generate more usage merely to make a cost appear in a screenshot.
Choose a checkpoint between sessions A good break follows a completed stack update and a result you can recover. After section 5.3, for example, record the stack, Region, queue names and test message ID. The next session can retrieve CloudFormation outputs and proceed to the worker. Leaving while a stack is rolling back makes the next session start with diagnosing that rollback.
Failure experiments spend time waiting for services. A queue message can be invisible, a workflow can be waiting for its next SES attempt, and CloudWatch needs a datapoint and an evaluation before an alarm changes state. Use that interval to record IDs and UTC times. Sending more messages during the wait changes the experiment.
Estimate activity from service operations An API call may enqueue a message, invoke Lambda and start several state transitions. A retry adds operations even when the order count stays constant. Record distinct orders, submissions, retries and log retention time alongside any billing estimate. These quantities help explain service-level charges later. Before leaving a session, identify which stacks the next session will need and which have finished their purpose.

title: Experiment procedure
content:
← Section contents
Prerequisites are AWS CLI v2, a stable source stack, a verified SES sender and a confirmed SNS email subscription. Use workshop-monitoring-5-6.json generated during setup. The script below records initial alarm/DLQ state and sends three messages with fresh IDs on each run.
Case Input Expected observations to check Success Valid SES simulator recipient SUCCEEDED execution and DONE order Email failure not-an-email Step Functions failure/retries, FAILED execution and sfn-failed alarm Malformed JSON not-json-mon56-… string Lambda JSON parsing failure, SQS retries and DLQ arrival With the section 5.5 code, Lambda returns after starting the workflow. A later SES failure need not increase Lambda Errors. Malformed JSON independently tests Lambda and the DLQ. An SQS MessageId proves acceptance, not processing completion.
& { param([string]$ConfigPath = (Join-Path $PWD.Path 'workshop-monitoring-5-6.json')) $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop' function Read-Aws([string[]]$Arguments) { $raw = & aws @Arguments --region $c.Region --output json --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw ('AWS CLI failed: '+($Arguments -join ' ')) } return (($raw -join [Environment]::NewLine) | ConvertFrom-Json) } try { $c = Get-Content -LiteralPath $ConfigPath -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json $id = 'mon56-'+(Get-Date -Format 'yyyyMMdd-HHmmss')+'-'+[guid]::NewGuid().ToString('N').Substring(0,6) $dir = Join-Path (Split-Path -Parent $ConfigPath) $id $null = New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $dir $utf8 = New-Object System.Text.UTF8Encoding($false) $before = Read-Aws -Arguments (@('cloudwatch','describe-alarms','--alarm-names') + @($c.AlarmNames)) [IO.File]::WriteAllText((Join-Path $dir 'alarms-before.json'),($before | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 30),$utf8) $queueBefore = Read-Aws -Arguments @('sqs','get-queue-attributes','--queue-url',$c.DlqUrl,'--attribute-names','ApproximateNumberOfMessages','ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible') [IO.File]::WriteAllText((Join-Path $dir 'dlq-before.json'),($queueBefore | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10),$utf8) Write-Host '=== ALARMS BEFORE TEST ===' -ForegroundColor Cyan $before.MetricAlarms | Select-Object AlarmName,StateValue | Format-Table -AutoSize $good = @{orderId=($id+'-ok');customerEmail='success@simulator.amazonses.com';acceptedAt=[DateTimeOffset]::UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds()} $bad = @{orderId=($id+'-ses-fail');customerEmail='not-an-email';acceptedAt=[DateTimeOffset]::UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds()} $cases = @( @{Name='success';Body=($good | ConvertTo-Json -Compress)}, @{Name='ses-failure';Body=($bad | ConvertTo-Json -Compress)}, @{Name='malformed-json';Body=('not-json-'+$id)} ) $results = @() foreach ($case in $cases) { $file = Join-Path $dir ($case.Name+'.txt') [IO.File]::WriteAllText($file,$case.Body,$utf8) $sent = Read-Aws -Arguments @('sqs','send-message','--queue-url',$c.QueueUrl,'--message-body',('file://'+$file)) $results += [pscustomobject]@{Case=$case.Name;MessageId=$sent.MessageId;SentAtUtc=[DateTimeOffset]::UtcNow.ToString('o')} [IO.File]::WriteAllText((Join-Path $dir 'sent.json'),($results | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10),$utf8) } $run = @{RunId=$id;GoodOrderId=$good.orderId;FailedOrderId=$bad.orderId;MalformedBody=('not-json-'+$id);EvidenceDirectory=$dir} [IO.File]::WriteAllText((Join-Path $dir 'run.json'),($run | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10),$utf8) Write-Host '=== TEST MESSAGES ACCEPTED BY SQS ===' -ForegroundColor Green $results | Format-Table -AutoSize $run | Format-List Write-Host 'Da gui 3 tin; chua ket luan xu ly thanh cong. Theo doi Step Functions, Lambda, DLQ va CloudWatch trong 5-10 phut.' Write-Host 'DLQ co san tin cu thi ALARM/email cu khong chung minh do tin vua gui.' } catch { Write-Host ('LOI: '+$_.Exception.Message) -ForegroundColor Red throw } } Observe for an initial 5–10 minutes and allow additional time for retries and metric publication. Find executions by orderId; correlate Lambda logs, the DLQ queue/body, alarm Details/History and matching email subjects. Do not use set-alarm-state as evidence of an actual application failure.
Predict the three signals before you send The valid simulator order can start a successful workflow. An invalid address is still valid JSON, so the worker can start the workflow before SES rejects the recipient. The third message stops at parsing. SQS can accept all three, but only the first two can start executions with a business ID. Search the Lambda log for the malformed text case.
One run keeps its payloads and send receipts together in a uniquely named directory. Inspect alarms-before.json to learn which alarms were already in ALARM. Read the visible and in-flight counts in dlq-before.json. Existing backlog is part of the baseline and can be left in place while interpreting the test.
Build a timeline after submission Milestone Source Use Send receipt sent.json and message ID Anchor the client’s observation of SQS acceptance Application failure Execution history or parsing log Associate the first failure with its case Alarm transition CloudWatch alarm history Identify a change that actually occurred Mailbox arrival SNS email naming the alarm Record arrival if measuring notification delivery Mark an unobserved milestone as pending and retain the others. Running the script again creates another three messages and a new set of IDs. Read the current results first, especially when a persistent ALARM state will not transition again for each message.
Reopen the observations without sending more messages Use the EvidenceDirectory printed by the run. The following block reads local data only. Match the rows in sent.json to the IDs in run.json. A run interrupted after its first accepted send may contain just one receipt. Include only cases with a recorded submission in that comparison.
$dir = Read-Host 'EvidenceDirectory' Get-Content -LiteralPath (Join-Path $dir 'sent.json') -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json | Format-Table Case, MessageId, SentAtUtc $runFile = Join-Path $dir 'run.json' if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $runFile) { Get-Content -LiteralPath $runFile -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json | Format-List } SentAtUtc was recorded after the send call returned and identifies a client-side observation. Keep it separate from the start of a Lambda invocation when building a detailed timeline. If an interruption prevented run.json from being written, retain the receipts and bodies already saved. Check their identifiers before repeating the experiment because some work may still finish on AWS.
Read worker logs for the submitted run Run from the application directory. Keep the run time beside the log window when distinguishing invocations from different trials.
$config = Get-Content -Raw -LiteralPath .\workshop-monitoring-5-6.json | ConvertFrom-Json aws logs tail $config.LogGroup --since 15m --region $config.Region --format short --no-cli-pager

title: Prepare the measurement tools
content:
← Section contents
In PowerShell, start in the order-system application directory and run the blocks in order. File writers use UTF-8 without a BOM. Save local customizations before replacing a file of the same name.
Prepare the tools directory and table client New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path .\tools -Force -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null Push-Location -LiteralPath .\tools -ErrorAction Stop try { if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath .\package.json)) { npm.cmd init -y if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'npm init failed.' } } npm.cmd install @aws-sdk/client-dynamodb @aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Dependency installation failed.' } } finally { Pop-Location } Submit requests and time the client response $content = @' const [target, prefix, countArg, workersArg, pauseArg = "0"] = process.argv.slice(2); const count = Number(countArg); const concurrency = Number(workersArg); const pauseMs = Number(pauseArg); const key = process.env.API_KEY; const customerEmail = process.env.CUSTOMER_EMAIL || "success@simulator.amazonses.com"; if (!target || !key || !/^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,54}$/.test(prefix ?? "") || !Number.isSafeInteger(count) || count < 1 || !Number.isInteger(concurrency) || concurrency < 1 || concurrency > count || !Number.isInteger(pauseMs) || pauseMs < 0) { console.error("Usage: loadtest.mjs <workshop-url> <prefix> <count> <concurrency> [pause-ms]. Set API_KEY."); process.exit(1); } const latencies = []; let accepted = 0, httpErrors = 0, networkErrors = 0; let next = 1; async function worker() { while (next <= count) { const orderId = `${prefix}-${next++}`; const body = JSON.stringify({ orderId, customerEmail }); const start = performance.now(); try { const response = await fetch(target, { method: "POST", headers: { "content-type": "application/json", "x-api-key": key }, body, signal: AbortSignal.timeout(30000), }); await response.text(); latencies.push(performance.now() - start); if (response.ok) accepted++; else httpErrors++; } catch { networkErrors++; } if (pauseMs && next <= count) await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, pauseMs)); } } await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: concurrency }, worker)); latencies.sort((a, b) => a - b); const samples = latencies.length; const mean = samples ? latencies.reduce((sum, ms) => sum + ms, 0) / samples : null; const p95 = samples ? latencies[Math.ceil(samples * 0.95) - 1] : null; console.table([{ prefix, count, concurrency, pauseMs, accepted, httpErrors, networkErrors, samples, avgMs: mean?.toFixed(2) ?? "N/A", p95Ms: p95?.toFixed(2) ?? "N/A" }]); if (httpErrors || networkErrors) process.exitCode = 2; '@ $path = Join-Path $PWD.Path 'tools/loadtest.mjs' [IO.File]::WriteAllText($path, ($content + [Environment]::NewLine), [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) Read order outcomes after submission $content = @' // Usage: node report.mjs <table-name> <prefix> <orders-sent> import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb"; import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, ScanCommand } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb"; const [table, prefix, n] = process.argv.slice(2); const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({})); const items = []; let key; do { const r = await db.send(new ScanCommand({ TableName: table, ConsistentRead: true, FilterExpression: "begins_with(orderId, :p)", ExpressionAttributeValues: { ":p": `${prefix}-` }, ExclusiveStartKey: key, })); items.push(...(r.Items ?? [])); key = r.LastEvaluatedKey; } while (key); const status = {}; for (const i of items) status[i.status] = (status[i.status] ?? 0) + 1; const extra = items.length && items.every(i => Number.isFinite(i.emailCount)) ? items.reduce((s, i) => s + Math.max(0, i.emailCount - 1), 0) : "N/A"; const d = items.filter(i => i.doneAt && i.createdAt) .map(i => Date.parse(i.doneAt) - i.createdAt).sort((a, b) => a - b); const avg = d.length ? Math.round(d.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0) / d.length) : null; const p95 = d.length ? d[Math.min(d.length - 1, Math.ceil(d.length * 0.95) - 1)] : null; console.log(`Prefix: ${prefix} | sent: ${n} | found: ${items.length} | not seen at read time: ${Number(n) - items.length}`); console.log("Status:", status); console.log("Extra emails (duplicates):", extra); console.log(`Completion time (ms): avg=${avg} p95=${p95} (orders: ${d.length})`); if (items.length <= 10) console.table(items.map(i => ({ orderId: i.orderId, status: i.status, emailCount: i.emailCount ?? "N/A" }))); '@ $path = Join-Path $PWD.Path 'tools/report.mjs' [IO.File]::WriteAllText($path, ($content + [Environment]::NewLine), [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) Read the two tools by input and output The load client accepts an endpoint URL, prefix, request count and worker concurrency. Each worker waits for a response, reads its body and records a client duration. Any configured pause between requests lies outside the latency sample. An HTTP error can have a measured response time. A network exception may produce no HTTP response at all. Report the timed sample count beside P95.
The report reads the table after submission. For a small lab table a paginated Scan with a prefix filter is convenient. Filtering does not reduce how many items DynamoDB must read before applying the filter. Run the report after allowing time for processing and check again if RECEIVED remains. Record both observation times instead of repeatedly scanning during the measurement.
Name populations and interpret missing values Use a timestamp, short unique suffix and the mode in the prefix. Distinct ...-sync and ...-async groups keep business IDs apart. Put warm-up requests under separate prefixes so the report excludes them. A missing doneAt or createdAt excludes the item from completion-time samples. A missing emailCount makes the extra-email measure unavailable. A missing value and a measured zero express different results.
Check both saved files locally before supplying a URL or key.
node --check .\tools\loadtest.mjs node --check .\tools\report.mjs

title: Preventing Duplicate Processing
content:
Objective An SQS queue guarantees at-least-once delivery, which means the same order may occasionally be delivered twice. If this is not handled, customers will receive duplicate emails. We use DynamoDB as a “ledger”: each orderId is processed only once. This technique is called idempotency.
Workshop steps Open a page below or use the sidebar. Follow the steps in order.
5.4.1 Update template.yaml 5.4.2 Write the Lambda code 5.4.3 Redeploy 5.4.4 Test 5.4.5 Verify the result 5.4.6 Troubleshooting

title: Test
content:
← Section contents
Set up the order ID and lookup targets $stackData = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Cannot read order-system.' } $outputs = @{} foreach ($item in ($stackData | Out-String | ConvertFrom-Json).Stacks[0].Outputs) { $outputs[$item.OutputKey] = $item.OutputValue } $q = $outputs['QueueUrl'] if (-not $q) { throw 'Missing output: QueueUrl' } $dlq = $outputs['DlqUrl'] if (-not $dlq) { throw 'Missing output: DlqUrl' } $table = $outputs['TableName'] if (-not $table) { throw 'Missing output: TableName' } 1. Submit an order and read by key $orderId = 'A-' + [guid]::NewGuid().ToString('N').Substring(0,10) $file = Join-Path $PWD.Path ("{0}.json" -f $orderId) $body = @{ orderId = $orderId } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress [IO.File]::WriteAllText($file, $body, [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body "file://$file" --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager Allow the worker time to process. If the first read has no Item, repeat just the read block.
$keyFile = Join-Path $PWD.Path 'workshop-item-key.json' $keyJson = @{ orderId = @{ S = $orderId } } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress [IO.File]::WriteAllText($keyFile, $keyJson, [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) aws dynamodb get-item --table-name $table --key "file://$keyFile" --consistent-read --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager 2. Resubmit the same saved payload aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body "file://$file" --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager sam logs --stack-name order-system --name ProcessOrderFn --region ap-southeast-1 --tail Wait for the duplicate log naming $orderId. Press Ctrl+C to end log tailing.
3. Trace an unreadable body $badBody = "not-json-$orderId" aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body $badBody --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager Allow several minutes for redelivery with the lab settings. Inspect the DLQ identified by $dlq for the exact body. In the recorded order-idempotency-evidence run the malformed body was khong-phai-json and the valid order was A001.
Sequence the duplicate test so it is interpretable The first send creates the item. Wait until PROCESSING is visible and note createdAt before sending the second request. Reuse the same JSON file. Changing the ID tests two valid orders. Conversely, reusing A001 from an older session can send even the first request down the duplicate branch. Choose a new ID for an independent run.
One DynamoDB row after two sends can also result from an unconditional overwrite to the same key. Pair a log line identifying the duplicate with the unchanged creation time. This version produces that combination when a conditional write succeeds and the next condition failure is handled.
Separate a parse failure from a table write failure The plain-text body in case 3 fails at JSON parsing before the worker can extract an orderId. Correlate it with the DLQ using a body marker and send time. A denied DynamoDB write can also lead to retries, but its log carries a different exception or action. Read the first error before editing the table settings. Record the observed body or matching log next to the run identifier.
Read a typed item in AWS CLI output In GetItem output, orderId.S contains a string ID, status.S contains PROCESSING and createdAt.N contains a number represented as text by the DynamoDB API. Two reads with the same key and creation value indicate the initial item survived. Pair this observation with the duplicate log to identify the worker decision on the second submission.
Illustrations from the recorded run Data in DynamoDB Lambda skips the resubmitted order A001 DynamoDB retains one A001 record after resubmission Invalid message found in the DLQ

title: Test a message falling into the DLQ
content:
← Section contents
Store the two queue URLs in variables:
$stackData = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Cannot read order-system.' } $outputs = @{} foreach ($item in ($stackData | Out-String | ConvertFrom-Json).Stacks[0].Outputs) { $outputs[$item.OutputKey] = $item.OutputValue } $q = $outputs['QueueUrl'] if (-not $q) { throw 'Missing output: QueueUrl' } $dlq = $outputs['DlqUrl'] if (-not $dlq) { throw 'Missing output: DlqUrl' } Send a test message:
$testBody = "test-dlq-$([guid]::NewGuid().ToString('N').Substring(0,10))" $testBody aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body $testBody --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager Receive the message several times without deleting it (the --visibility-timeout 0 parameter makes the message visible again immediately):
1..4 | ForEach-Object { aws sqs receive-message --queue-url $q --visibility-timeout 0 --wait-time-seconds 2 --message-system-attribute-names ApproximateReceiveCount --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager Start-Sleep -Seconds 1 } SQS can move the message once actual receives cross the threshold. Wait about a minute, then check the DLQ:
aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url $dlq --attribute-names ApproximateNumberOfMessages --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager Or go to the Console → the DLQ queue → Send and receive messages → Poll for messages.
SQS metrics are approximate and may be delayed by several tens of seconds.
Give the experiment a recognizable message Use the lab queues before attaching the worker in section 5.4. An active consumer could process and delete the test message before your manual poll. Give the body a run-specific marker and keep the MessageId returned by SQS. An older DLQ item can make its count positive even before this run.
The receive loop sets the visibility timeout to zero for these individual receives. That makes redelivery possible quickly while leaving the source queue’s configured 60 seconds intact. Leave the message undeleted. Each response containing the matching body counts as an observed delivery. An empty poll is also possible with a Standard queue.
Interpret the end of the polling loop If the new body appears in the DLQ, record the run marker, message ID and destination name. If the source still contains it, check how many matching deliveries occurred and inspect the redrive policy before polling again. If both visible counts temporarily read zero, allow for metric lag. Polling the DLQ to inspect a body is itself a receive operation and can hide the item for a visibility interval.
This experiment establishes redelivery behavior for one message. In the next chapter a failing Lambda invocation supplies the reason for retry. Here the manual receive without deletion supplies that condition.

title: Testing
content:
← Section contents
Prepare a test run $stackData = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Cannot read order-system.' } $outputs = @{} foreach ($item in ($stackData | Out-String | ConvertFrom-Json).Stacks[0].Outputs) { $outputs[$item.OutputKey] = $item.OutputValue } $q = $outputs['QueueUrl'] if (-not $q) { throw 'Missing output: QueueUrl' } $table = $outputs['TableName'] if (-not $table) { throw 'Missing output: TableName' } $tag = [guid]::NewGuid().ToString('N').Substring(0,10) $goodId = "B001-$tag" $failId = "B002-$tag" $email = Read-Host 'Verified test inbox for the order confirmation' 1. Trace the successful order $file = Join-Path $PWD.Path ("{0}.json" -f $goodId) $body = @{ orderId = $goodId; customerEmail = $email } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress [IO.File]::WriteAllText($file, $body, [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body "file://$file" --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager $goodFile = $file $goodId Find $goodId in Step Functions and then read its item. After the execution succeeds, check for DONE and a matching email subject.
$keyFile = Join-Path $PWD.Path 'workshop-item-key.json' $keyJson = @{ orderId = @{ S = $goodId } } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress [IO.File]::WriteAllText($keyFile, $keyJson, [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) aws dynamodb get-item --table-name $table --key "file://$keyFile" --consistent-read --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager 2. Resubmit the same body aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body "file://$goodFile" --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager sam logs --stack-name order-system --name ProcessOrderFn --region ap-southeast-1 --tail Wait for the duplicate log and press Ctrl+C.
3. Follow a rejected SES task In the SES sandbox an unverified normal recipient is rejected. This block uses a malformed address to give a failure case even with production access.
$email = 'not-an-email' $file = Join-Path $PWD.Path ("{0}.json" -f $failId) $body = @{ orderId = $failId; customerEmail = $email } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress [IO.File]::WriteAllText($file, $body, [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body "file://$file" --region ap-southeast-1 --output json --no-cli-pager $failId Find execution $failId. After retries inspect MarkFailed, NotifyAdminFailure, the FAILED item and the administrative email for that ID. The original figures show B001 and B002.

title: Verify your email in Amazon SES

← Section contents
In the SES sandbox, use a verified sender identity. Recipients can be verified addresses or SES mailbox simulator addresses.
Go to Amazon SES → Identities → Create identity. Choose Email address, enter your email, and select Create identity. Open the verification email from AWS and click the link. The identity status changes to Verified. Why email preparation matters SES sends customer confirmations. Sandbox status and identity verification apply per Region. An address verified in another Region is not sufficient for a workflow running in Singapore.
In the sandbox, ordinary sender and recipient addresses must meet verification requirements. SES mailbox simulator addresses are an exception for testing. Production access removes the requirement to verify recipients individually, while sender identities still need to be valid.
Check account status aws sesv2 get-account --region ap-southeast-1 --query '{Production:ProductionAccessEnabled,Sending:SendingEnabled}' --output json --no-cli-pager Production=false indicates sandbox status. Production=true indicates production access; Sending reports whether account-level sending is enabled. This command only reads information: it neither sends mail nor requests production access.
Prepare a test recipient Open SES in Singapore and inspect Verified identities. If a new address is needed, create its email identity and have the mailbox owner follow the AWS verification link. Wait for Verified before submitting a new test order.
SNS subscription confirmation and SES identity verification are separate actions. Confirming an SNS subscription does not verify the address in SES. success@simulator.amazonses.com supports successful send-task tests but does not provide a recipient inbox for a delivered-email screenshot.
The verification screenshot below does not display a Region or the account’s production-access status. Check those separately before drawing conclusions about sending to other recipients.
Email verification evidence Amazon SES lists vuhungmanhjr2k5@gmail.com as an Email address identity with Verified status.This confirms verification in the displayed identity list. The screenshot does not show the Region or production-access status. Check ap-southeast-1 and sandbox status separately before sending to another recipient. Verified does not establish successful submission or delivery of an order confirmation.
Check the address that will send mail Enter the email identity verified in your lab account. The following command reads its Singapore identity record. Look for VerifiedForSendingStatus set to true before supplying this address as the deployment parameter SenderEmail. The example uses an individual email identity as created above.
$sender = Read-Host 'SES sender email' aws sesv2 get-email-identity --email-identity $sender --region ap-southeast-1 --query '{Type:IdentityType,VerifiedForSendingStatus:VerifiedForSendingStatus}' --output table --no-cli-pager For NotFoundException, check the Region and the spelling of the address. For a pending identity, open the matching mailbox and follow the current AWS verification link. Keep a note of the sender and recipient roles used in your test so the deployment prompts are easy to complete.
Select the recipient for the question you are testing Use the success simulator when measuring the API and checking whether SES accepted a task. title: Workshop
content:
Workshop overview This workshop builds an asynchronous order-processing system on AWS, with the Moc storefront as a demonstration application. A visitor selects a product, enters an email address and submits an order. The backend accepts the request, processes it, sends notifications and stores a status that the visitor can track.
The objective goes beyond sending an email. The system must distinguish accepted requests from completed orders, handle messages delivered more than once, and help an operator investigate failures. The workshop therefore combines queues, a database, orchestration and monitoring.
Main components Component group Responsibility SQS and DLQ Buffer incoming requests and retain messages that meet the redrive failure conditions Lambda and DynamoDB Process requests, control duplicates and store order status Step Functions Coordinate tasks and apply the configured Retry/Catch behavior SES and SNS Send customer confirmations and administrator notifications CloudWatch Collect logs and metrics, display dashboards and evaluate alarms Demonstration and verification Moc is an experimental storefront without payments, inventory management or real deliveries. Follow the same order ID through the website, DynamoDB, Step Functions execution and confirmation email. DONE indicates that the application workflow completed; inbox delivery requires a separate check.
The exercises progress from environment preparation to successful processing, duplicate requests, controlled failures and cleanup. Distinguish observed results from expected outcomes. A successful deployment screenshot alone does not demonstrate successful end-to-end processing.
An optional product-page screenshot can introduce the demonstration. There is no need to submit another order just to capture the storefront. Present processing evidence in the experiment sections.
Workshop contents 5.1 Introduction and Architecture 5.2 Preparation (IAM, Region, Tools) 5.3 Queues and DLQ 5.4 Preventing Duplicate Processing 5.5 Orchestration and Notifications 5.6 Monitoring 5.7 Fault and Load Experiments 5.8 Clean up

title: Experiment 1: latency and load
content:
← Section contents
On November 13, 2026, two APIs in order-api-evidence were tested using the DynamoDB table and workflow in order-orchestration-evidence. Run ID: cmp-20261113160505330-eac6bb.
Each mode used 20 measured requests, concurrency 1, a 1,500 ms pause after each response, and two excluded warm-up requests. Synchronous ran first, then asynchronous. Recipient: success@simulator.amazonses.com. The actual tool was workshop-benchmark-tools/compare.cjs; illustrative tools above may use a different output format.
Synchronous results Asynchronous results Asynchronous results for 20 orders
Comparison Metric Synchronous Asynchronous Measured requests / concurrency 20 / 1 20 / 1 Pause after response (ms) 1500 1500 Successful HTTP requests 20/20 20/20 HTTP / network errors 0 / 0 0 / 0 Average API latency (ms) 229.55 109.28 P95 API latency (ms) 343.33 110.62 Records found / DONE 20 / 20 20 / 20 FAILED / other / not observed 0 / 0 / 0 0 / 0 / 0 Completion timestamp samples 20 20 Average approximate completion (ms) 122.75 445.55 P95 approximate completion (ms) 138 516 Comparison with matching test settings
Observation: the asynchronous API responded faster in this run, while approximate completion took longer. HTTP 202 confirms acceptance; DONE is checked separately in DynamoDB. Client API latency excludes the pacing pause. Approximate completion uses application createdAt and doneAt, with different measurement boundaries; it is neither inbox delivery time nor exact Step Functions duration.
This is one small paced test per mode, not a maximum-throughput measurement. Equal pauses after responses do not ensure equal arrival rates. Downloads/workshop-api-evidence.json contains an API key and must not be published.
Repeat the measurement on your stack Work in order-system using the session that set $api, $table and the key in 5.7.3. This block uses the two endpoints belonging to the workshop stack. Each path uses two warm-ups with separate IDs. The example client in 5.7.4 supports a 1,500 ms pause after a response and before the next request. Your output is a new run. The original table identifies its own benchmark tool and date.
$runId = 'cmp-' + [guid]::NewGuid().ToString('N').Substring(0,10) $env:CUSTOMER_EMAIL = 'success@simulator.amazonses.com' foreach ($mode in 'sync','async') { $prefix = "$runId-$mode" node .\tools\loadtest.mjs "$api/$mode" "$prefix-warm" 2 1 1500 if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "Warm-up failed for $mode." } Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 1500 node .\tools\loadtest.mjs "$api/$mode" "$prefix-measured" 20 1 1500 if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "Check the run for $mode before continuing." } Get-Date -Format o node .\tools\report.mjs $table "$prefix-measured" 20 if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Report failed.' } } If the async report still shows RECEIVED or some IDs are absent, allow more processing time and rerun only the report with the same prefix. Repeating the whole block creates new orders. For 20 timed responses nearest-rank P95 is the nineteenth sorted value. A network exception can reduce the timed sample count below 20.
Get-Date -Format o node .\tools\report.mjs $table "$runId-async-measured" 20 Read both differences in the recorded table Mean API latency went from 229.55 to 109.28 ms, a difference of 120.27 ms in this run. Approximate mean completion time went from 122.75 to 445.55 ms, a difference of 322.80 ms in the other direction. The async API responded while downstream work was still underway. Both groups eventually contained 20 completed items. A different concurrency or SES throttling regime calls for a separate table with its own conditions and observation time.

The test message contains run ID mon56-20261114-040056-316515. Dashboard/alarm times are UTC; the inbox and SQS timestamps shown use UTC+07:00. For example, November 13, 2026, 21:03:44 UTC equals November 14, 2026, 04:03:44 UTC+07:00.

The inbox screenshot establishes receipt of the ALARM notification, consistent with the CloudWatch alarm state. Reconstruct the sequence from recorded times Sort the events in UTC first. The DLQ transition at 21:01:06 UTC relates to a datapoint preceding the new malformed message. The Lambda transition at 21:02:21 UTC indicates Errors crossed its threshold. The Step Functions transition at 21:03:44 UTC indicates a period with one failed execution. This orders the alarms. Linking an invocation to an individual message still requires application evidence.
For example, the DLQ body containing mon56-20261114-040056-316515 connects the run directly to its destination. The Errors graph aggregates events. A rise around the same time points to a useful log window but carries no message ID. Keep both timestamps if a dashboard view and an alarm detail view were captured at different times.
Record your own observations Field Source Run ID and malformed marker The run directory’s run.json DLQ baseline dlq-before.json Alarm and before/after states Baseline, alarm history and received email First workflow failure Execution for the -ses-fail order Missing milestone Name the unavailable source, such as mailbox arrival time A metric timestamp identifies a statistical period. Computing detection latency needs both the actual failure and the alarm transition on the same clock basis. Measuring mail delivery needs a corresponding receipt. Limit conclusions from the recorded run to the milestones available.
Read an alarm email from top to bottom Start with the alarm name and Region to identify the deployment. Read the previous and new states, then the transition reason. The reason describes the datapoint that crossed the threshold and its evaluation period. Finally record the state change time. A mailbox can display local time, so retain the offset when comparing it with CloudWatch UTC.
The recorded Lambda and Step Functions transitions were 83 seconds apart, from 21:02:21 to 21:03:44 UTC. That subtraction describes the spacing between two alarm transitions from different services. It cannot measure how long Lambda took to detect its own fault or how long an email took to arrive. Two accurate timestamps can answer the wrong question if they describe the wrong milestones.
A reference to the matching alarm detail or existing figure, plus the alarm name and time, is sufficient for a reader to follow the timeline without opening every illustration.

title: Orchestration and Notifications
content:
Objective Instead of letting a single Lambda function do everything, we use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the order-processing workflow. The email task defines Retry and Catch behavior, the state of every order is recorded, and administrators are notified immediately through Amazon SNS when an order fails.
Workflow:
Lambda receives a message from SQS, records it in DynamoDB (RECEIVED), and starts the state machine. The state machine sends a confirmation email to the customer using Amazon SES (up to 3 retries). On success: update the status to DONE. On failure: update the status to FAILED, send an alert through SNS, and end in a failed state. Workshop steps Open a page below or use the sidebar. title: Set up a cost alert
content:
← Section contents
Go to Billing and Cost Management → Budgets → Create budget. Choose Zero spend budget or Monthly cost budget (for example, 5 USD). Enter the email to receive alerts. Purpose of a budget AWS Budgets compares costs against a configured amount. Select a budget suitable for the lab; an example amount is not a guaranteed estimate of the workshop’s final cost.
Budget notifications can be delayed and do not automatically stop all resources when a threshold is reached. Combine notifications with resource reviews and cleanup.
Configuration to review The budget type and reporting period. The selected amount and notification thresholds. The intended notification email address. The scope: the whole account or a configured filter/tag selection. Account-wide costs may include unrelated activity. Cost Explorer screenshots should show the date range and filters. Delayed or rounded figures do not establish that a lab is entirely free.
After the exercise Record stacks, buckets, log groups and retained resources. Clean up after evidence has been saved and the website is no longer needed for a demonstration. Do not generate extra emails or resources merely to populate a cost chart.
The supplied screenshot shows the workshop budget amount and its displayed status. It does not show actual spending, the reporting period, notification recipients or evidence that an alert email was delivered.
Budget configuration evidence order-workshop-budget is configured at USD 5; the list shows Thresholds OK and Health status Healthy.USD 5 is the configured budget amount, not actual spending. My Monthly Cost Budget at USD 100 is a separate budget in the list. This screenshot does not show the reporting period, detailed notification thresholds, recipient email or delivery of an alert. Open order-workshop-budget to review those settings.
Interpret a monthly threshold For a worked example, a USD 5 monthly budget with an alert at 80% of actual cost has a USD 4 threshold within its scope. A Forecasted threshold evaluates the expected cost for the whole period. The same percentage can therefore produce notifications at different times. Record Actual or Forecasted alongside the amount.
If the account hosts other applications, inspect the budget filter first. An account-wide notification cannot identify which stack caused the increase. Select the matching dates in Cost Explorer, group by service and connect a change to an activity in the lab. Repeated delivery of malformed messages, for example, can increase worker invocations.
Respond to a budget email Record when you received the email and which billing period it covers. Check whether a test is still running, a stack is being kept for a demonstration, or a dashboard or log group is still needed. After cleanup allow for billing data to refresh before checking new charges. The period, threshold, scope and follow-up decision make a useful written record.

title: Verify the result
content:
← Section contents
There are two queues, and the main queue points to the DLQ with maxReceiveCount = 3. A message received more than 3 times without being deleted ends up in the DLQ. Combine a configuration result with a delivery result Use two rows for acceptance. The configuration row contains the redrive destination, actual DLQ ARN and maxReceiveCount. The behavior row identifies the test body, at least one matching source receive and the destination where you found the same body. This lets a reader distinguish a configured failure path from a message actually observed on that path.
Observation Interpretation Next check Destination matches and the test body is in the DLQ Configuration and transfer were observed for this run Record the time and finish the test DLQ count increased but the body is unidentified A message is waiting Look for the run marker A source message is in flight A visibility interval is active Recheck after it expires No successful source receives The experiment has not reached the receive threshold Verify the source URL and active consumers Hand the queues over to the worker Record whether any test message remains in the source. Once the trigger is enabled, Lambda can immediately receive an earlier plain-text body. A parse error just after deployment may belong to that item. Its body and send time distinguish it from a new order in 5.4.4. A message already in the DLQ remains subject to its own handling and retention.

Case Expected result Valid order One row in DynamoDB Duplicate send The log reports a duplicate, no new row is added Message that is not JSON After a few retries, the message ends up in the DLQ Make one record for each case Fill in values from your own run. A MessageId traces an individual send, while orderId identifies the purchase. The duplicate case can yield two different message IDs for one order. For malformed input, record the body marker instead of an order ID. The case remains traceable even when the worker cannot create an item.
Evidence New order Resubmission Invalid body Identity Fresh order ID, first message ID Same order ID, second message ID Body marker and message ID Table change createdAt and PROCESSING appear Compare with original creation time Parsing stops before the write Deciding observation Processing log for this ID Duplicate branch in the log Parse error and matching body in the DLQ Resolve incomplete observations If the item exists but no duplicate log is visible, check the log window, stream and function. If the log is present but a table read appears stale, use a consistent read by key. An older body in the DLQ leaves the current malformed case pending. Record these results before advancing to orchestration, where the states acquire different meanings.
Reopen a single order in a fresh PowerShell session Enter the ID from the observation table. This request uses the primary key and strong consistency. For a response without Item, check the ID, table and Region before submitting another message.

OK with notBreaching does not independently establish application health. Examine an apparent return to OK Suppose an operator polls the DLQ to inspect a body. The visible count can fall during the visibility interval even though the message remains. Without a breaching point in the next period, the alarm may return to OK. To establish business recovery, check how the item was handled, the final order state and whether the message returned after the visibility timeout.
An interval without Lambda Errors can likewise occur with no traffic at all. Read Invocations and trace a valid order over the same interval. A workflow that is still retrying has not yet registered a terminal failed execution.
Bound the conclusion in the report Use three sentences. Start with a direct observation, such as a matching test body in the expected DLQ. State an explanation that still needs evidence, such as a possible link between a Lambda error datapoint and a parse failure. Finish with the observation that could distinguish it, such as the timestamped log entry and message ID. This format works with text-only evidence.
Leave detection latency blank when the initiating error was not timestamped. Mark recovery as untested when it was not observed. These limits identify the additional data needed before turning a lab observation into an operational commitment.
Design a later recovery check Choose the specific capability that should recover. For an SES identity issue, the objective could be a new order with a valid recipient reaching DONE after correction. For the DLQ, it could be a particular message investigated, corrected at the input and handled under the application’s recovery process. Sending the same malformed text back to the source would encounter the same parse failure.
Identify a starting observation, intervention and checkable end state. For example, record the failed order, correct the test recipient in a new payload, submit a fresh ID and check the email task and table update. Label this as a check of new traffic after a correction. The older item still describes the original failure.
Open question Evidence needed in a later run How long did detection take? Timestamped original fault and corresponding alarm transition How long did notification delivery take? Same notification, transition time and inbox receipt time Was the backlog resolved? Message identifiers, final handling outcome and an observation after the visibility timeout This table is a measurement plan. Enter recovery results only after the corresponding run has taken place.

title: Experiment 2: duplicate orders

Identical messages for dup-proof-20261113-220937-a7468d were submitted to SQS five times. Results: execution SUCCEEDED, one successful SES task in that execution, DynamoDB DONE, and emailCount = 1.
Logs show duplicates being skipped. Two workflow-started log lines do not establish two executions: Standard StartExecution with the same name and input can return an existing running execution.
Logs showing duplicate orders skipped
The inbox received a confirmation with the matching order ID. These observations support duplicate handling in this test, not guaranteed exactly-once email delivery under all failures.
Received confirmation email
Replay one purchase with a stable identity The recorded trial submitted one body directly to SQS five times. This exercises the downstream worker and workflow. The intake API is outside this particular test. For a repeat, choose a verified test inbox to observe email delivery or the simulator to observe only SES task success. $q = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='QueueUrl'].OutputValue | [0]" --region ap-southeast-1 --output text --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0 -or $q -eq 'None') { throw 'QueueUrl unavailable.' } $dupId = 'dup-' + [guid]::NewGuid().ToString('N').Substring(0,10) $email = Read-Host 'Verified test recipient (Enter = SES simulator)' if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($email)) { $email = 'success@simulator.amazonses.com' } $body = @{ orderId = $dupId; customerEmail = $email } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress $file = Join-Path $PWD.Path "$dupId.json" [IO.File]::WriteAllText($file, $body, [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) 1..5 | ForEach-Object { aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body "file://$file" --region ap-southeast-1 --query MessageId --output text --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "Send $_ failed." } } $dupId Each accepted send returns a message ID. For a real inbox, find the subject containing the fresh ID. Reading results requires no sixth submission.
Investigate counts that disagree For two “started” log lines, count distinct execution ARNs first. For one execution with multiple successful SES tasks, inspect state history, timing and retries. For a single item with a counter greater than one, verify the template version and run ID. Each observation narrows the next investigation. title: Troubleshooting
content:
← Section contents
Lambda does not run: go to Console → Lambda → the ProcessOrderFn function → Configuration → Triggers tab, and check that the SQS trigger is Enabled. DynamoDB permission error: check the log, and make sure the Policies section of the template uses the correct !Ref OrdersTable. sam logs shows nothing: wait a few seconds and send the message again, as logs have a small delay. Narrow the search from queue to table Start with a fresh order ID and a UTC send time. Confirm that SQS returned a message ID. Then look for an invocation of the intended function in the same interval. Visible messages with an inactive mapping point to the trigger. A fall in visible count with an increase in in-flight messages can mean processing is underway or a failed delivery is waiting for its visibility timeout.
sam logs --stack-name order-system --name ProcessOrderFn --region ap-southeast-1 --start-time '15min ago' Look for the ID or the first exception near its send time. For Runtime.ImportModuleError inspect the handler file, CodeUri and packaged dependencies. For denied PutItem access check the execution role and table ARN. A handled conditional write failure is expected for a duplicate. Keep the time alongside the observation because one stream can contain many orders.
Verify a correction with a small case Change one factor at a time. Rebuild and update the same stack after a code or template edit. Changing a log filter only requires reading the log again. To recheck new-order processing, use a fresh ID. To test the duplicate branch, intentionally reuse the ID. Record the original symptom, change made and observed outcome. These three lines document a reproducible repair.

title: Troubleshooting
content:
← Section contents
Not receiving the order confirmation email: check that both SenderEmail and the customer email are Verified in SES, and check your spam folder. Not receiving the alert: check whether you clicked Confirm subscription in SNS (Console → SNS → Subscriptions, the status must be Confirmed). No execution at all: check the ProcessOrderFn logs; if there is a permissions error, review the Policies section in the template. Execution reports an AccessDenied error at SES: check that the state machine’s role has ses:SendEmail. Trace the symptom to the responsible service For a missing confirmation, start with the customer’s order ID. A missing item leads back to the queue and worker. A RECEIVED item leads to the execution name. Once an execution is found, inspect the final state reached and the first failure. This sequence avoids changing SES verification when the worker has not yet started the state machine.
If the SES task reports access denied, inspect the state machine role and the allowed action. If SES reports an unverified identity, check the sender, test recipient and Region. For rate limiting after a burst, read retry history before submitting again manually. A manual resend adds another request to the experiment and can obscure the original cause.
Investigate FAILED with no administrative email Find NotifyAdminFailure in execution history. If it was never reached, inspect the preceding table update. For a denied publish, identify the role and topic ARN from the error. For a successful publish, check the confirmed subscription, inbox and spam folder of the intended administrative address. Record the last confirmed step before attributing the incident.
After the correction, use a fresh test order. Keep the old execution as a reference for comparison. The old ID, new ID and single change between runs document the repair.

title: Sharing and Feedback

Overall Impressions and Evaluation 1. Working Environment
During my internship, I found the working environment friendly, open, and supportive of interns taking the initiative to learn. I could focus on my assigned tasks while also having room to explore AWS topics I had never worked with before. What I valued most was that the environment did not put too much pressure on me, yet still expected everyone to be self-disciplined and responsible for their own work.

I ran into quite a few Cloud-related problems, as well as some unrelated ones, and the mentors and admins always helped me enthusiastically. In particular, the Cloud knowledge they shared during the workshop sessions and while I was working on the workshop taught me that it is not enough to make a system work. I also need to explain why I chose a particular service and how the services connect to each other. As a result, I gradually improved the way I think about and present a technical solution.

I am majoring in Computer Networks and Communications, so before joining the program my knowledge mostly covered networking, network administration, and some systems knowledge. When I started learning AWS, I saw that Cloud has many topics related to what I had already studied, such as servers, storage, access control, networking, and system monitoring, but the way they are implemented in practice has many new aspects.
While working on the project “Building a Backup & Recovery System for a Web Server on AWS”, I had the chance to combine my server and networking knowledge with Cloud services such as EC2, EBS, S3, IAM, AWS Backup, and CloudWatch. This helped me better understand how what I learned at school can be applied in a Cloud environment.

The internship let me learn a lot that I had not studied in depth before, especially Cloud services. While working on the project, I did not just follow instructions. I also had to research documentation, debug errors, and try several different configurations before getting the result I wanted.

I felt the working environment values initiative and self-learning. Each intern is responsible for their own progress, but when facing difficulties, they can still discuss them and get support.
This helped me gradually build the habit of investigating a problem on my own first, then gathering the parts I could not solve to discuss with others. During the internship, I was given the opportunity to learn new knowledge while practicing directly on AWS. I appreciate that the program does not only require completing a project, but also includes sharing sessions, guidance, and reviews that help interns better understand how real work is done.
Gaining access to Cloud knowledge, practicing directly with AWS services, and attending knowledge-sharing sessions while working on the project were valuable experiences for me. Through this internship, I have a clearer direction for continuing to study AWS, Cloud Computing, and topics related to my major in Computer Networks and Communications.
As a coffee lover, I especially enjoyed the coffee corner at the office, which gave me plenty of energy and kept me alert for studying.

A not-json-... body fails at the worker parser and never reaches the email state. Keep separate markers so you do not search for a workflow execution that could never start.
$q = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='QueueUrl'].OutputValue | [0]" --region ap-southeast-1 --output text --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0 -or $q -eq 'None') { throw 'QueueUrl unavailable.' } $tag = [guid]::NewGuid().ToString('N').Substring(0,10) $failedId = "ses-fail-$tag" $badBody = "not-json-$tag" $file = Join-Path $PWD.Path "$failedId.json" $body = @{ orderId = $failedId; customerEmail = 'not-an-email' } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress [IO.File]::WriteAllText($file, $body, [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body "file://$file" --region ap-southeast-1 --query MessageId --output text --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'First send failed.' } aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body $badBody --region ap-southeast-1 --query MessageId --output text --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Second send failed.' } [pscustomobject]@{ OrderId = $failedId; DlqMarker = $badBody } For the first case, inspect the first error, task reschedules, table update and NotifyAdminFailure publish. The 5.7 template permits six retries, so allow for backoff before checking the terminal state. A recorded environment may have different retry settings. Count events for the run you actually inspect. For the second case, find $badBody in the application’s DLQ and check the corresponding alarm from 5.6.
Capture comparable timestamps Separating detection time and mail delivery needs the initial error from history or a log, the alarm transition and the inbox arrival. Convert all three to UTC before subtracting. The SNS notification timestamp describes a service event and may differ from mailbox receipt. If the DLQ was already in alarm, the new item can arrive without a new state-transition email. Record that as a valid observation of the configured alarm behavior.

$monitorStack = 'order-monitoring' aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name $monitorStack --region ap-southeast-1 --query 'Stacks[0].{Stack:StackName,Status:StackStatus}' --output table --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Check the monitoring stack name and Region.' } if ((Read-Host "Type $monitorStack to remove this lab monitoring stack") -ceq $monitorStack) { aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name $monitorStack --region ap-southeast-1 if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Deletion request failed.' } aws cloudformation wait stack-delete-complete --stack-name $monitorStack --region ap-southeast-1 if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Inspect stack events before continuing.' } } 1. Delete the main stack sam delete --stack-name order-system --region ap-southeast-1 Answer y to the confirmation prompts. This command deletes the CloudFormation stack together with SQS, the DLQ, DynamoDB, Lambda, Step Functions, SNS, other resources in this stack, and the HTTP API.
Check that the latest deployment of the stack is DELETE_COMPLETE. CloudFormation can retain earlier stack history.
aws cloudformation list-stacks --region ap-southeast-1 --query "StackSummaries[?StackName=='order-system'].[StackName,StackStatus,CreationTime]" --output table --no-cli-pager 2. Delete the Lambda log groups Lambda creates its log groups automatically, so they are not deleted with the stack:
$groups = aws logs describe-log-groups --region ap-southeast-1 --log-group-name-prefix '/aws/lambda/order-system-' --query 'logGroups[].logGroupName' --output json --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Cannot list log groups.' } foreach ($name in ($groups | Out-String | ConvertFrom-Json)) { if ((Read-Host "Type DELETE to remove the lab log group $name") -ceq 'DELETE') { aws logs delete-log-group --region ap-southeast-1 --log-group-name $name if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "Could not delete $name." } } } 3. 4. Delete the verified email in SES (optional) Go to Amazon SES → Identities → select the email → Delete.

Go to IAM → Users → select the user → Security credentials → Deactivate and then Delete the access key. Detach the OrderWorkshopDeployPolicy policy from the user, then delete the policy if it is no longer needed. Remove the profile from your machine: open the %USERPROFILE%\.aws\credentials and config files and delete the order-workshop section. Remove the environment variables in PowerShell: Remove-Item Env:API_KEY, Env:CUSTOMER_EMAIL -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue 6. title: Conclusion
content:
← Section contents
Both modes reached DONE for 20/20 orders in this run. Separate tests recorded duplicate handling, SES retries, SNS failure notifications and DLQ alerts. Findings are limited to the documented test conditions and runs.
Choose the architecture using both timelines For a customer waiting at checkout, the relevant interval begins when the client sends the request and ends on intake confirmation. In the recorded run both groups had 20 successful HTTP responses. Client-side means were 229.55 ms for sync and 109.28 ms for async. The async storefront can immediately present the order ID and acceptance status. Reporting completion at that point would get ahead of the workflow.
For support staff checking progress, the relevant observation is the final DONE or FAILED for that ID. Approximate mean completion was 122.75 ms for sync and 445.55 ms for async in the measured groups. Those times come from application fields. Their relationship to client latency depends on clock boundaries and how much work continues outside the request. Treating them as interchangeable leads to incorrect status messages.
Link the conclusion to the experiment Experiment Recorded observation Scope Small API run 20/20 DONE for each mode at concurrency one Async intake responded faster in the recorded conditions Five sends of one body One verified execution, one successful SES task, counter one Duplicate handling worked for that ID and scenario Rejected email Error, retry and administrative path in history A failure after acceptance can be traced Malformed body Matching DLQ body and an observed alarm Failed input can be retained for investigation Incident notification latency Matching timestamp pair unavailable The interval remains unmeasured Include submitted requests, distinct order IDs, the observation time and actual sample count with a comparison. Treat a change of recipient type or worker concurrency as a new run. Retain the original population as a reference.
Hand over results before cleanup Choose one successful and one failed order you actually submitted. For each, record the API path or queue source, final state, evidence inspected and any open question. For invalid input lacking an order ID, use the body marker and DLQ name. Together with the latency table, these records let another reader check the reasoning without opening your AWS account.
Before section 5.8 removes resources, save the prefixes, benchmark output and final observation time. This matters for logs and items belonging to the stack that will be removed. Billing needs its own check for newly accrued charges. A configured budget or a small value on a single billing view does not supply that measurement.
Revisit the conclusion when the business requirement changes A merchant who needs only “request received” while the customer is at checkout can evaluate the first screen using API latency and a traceable order ID. The customer can check the final state afterward. If the success screen promises that the email was submitted and processing was recorded, the measurement must extend to completion. The recorded table supplies two distinct intervals for that decision.
Another requirement might give the operator a notification deadline. Received emails establish that a notification channel worked on the observed run. The missing timestamp of the initiating fault still prevents a fault-to-notification measurement. Name which requirement was exercised and which needs an additional observation. A later run can use the same resources while recording the original error time and correlating alarm history with the corresponding inbox message.
Write a result paragraph from a new run “Run … in Singapore used … distinct orders per mode at concurrency …. API mean/P95 were … for sync and … for async. At … UTC the table contained … DONE, … FAILED and … pending. Order … demonstrated the failure path at state …. The … measure lacks source or timestamp ….” Fill the fields from observations and leave unresolved fields open. This places conditions, measurements and limitations together for a fair comparison with the recorded run.
